7. The FDV ratchet enforces a minimum TWAP window
with no maximum
Acknowledged
Path
contracts/LPFeeRatchet.sol, contracts/TokenSplitter.sol
Function Name
poke(), TokenSplitter._creatorBps()
poke() reverts only when the observed span is below TWAP_WINDOW (LPFeeRatchet.sol:168-169);
there is no maximum-window cap. If poke goes uncalled after a window matures, or trading is
sparse enough that the hook's last observation advances only occasionally, the committed
average is computed over however long the window has actually been open, potentially far longer
than 24 hours, diluting recent price movement with stale data.
Impact
Because the tier function is a step function, a diluted average can hold the split at the higher
creator tier materially longer than the schedule intends. TokenSplitter._creatorBps reads the live
tier on every LP-fee deposit, so the creator keeps receiving the pre-ratchet share of every harvest
for the duration of the over-long window: a real, bounded, self-correcting transfer from treasury to
creator
Likelihood
Medium in keeper-liveness terms, but mitigated. poke is permissionless, so any keeper can call it
the moment a window matures, capping typical exposure near 24 hours.
Recommendation
Enforce a maximum span, for example twice TWAP_WINDOW, and reopen the window instead of
committing when it is exceeded, or snapshot fixed windows automatically.
CrackerSwap Team’s Comment
The window span is measured in observed time, which only swaps advance, so a pool trading once
a month legitimately has a month-long window. Any cap tight enough to matter would re-anchor
those windows forever, permanently favouring the creator, which is the opposite of the finding's
intent. The fix for issue 4 mitigates this instead: every harvest now pokes the ratchet, so windows
close promptly rather than growing stale.

8. The FDV ratchet reads only the single hooked V4
pool, blind to other venues
Acknowledged
Path
contracts/LPFeeRatchet.sol
Function Name
poolKeyOf(), poke()
poolKeyOf hardcodes a single pool key, native ETH against the launch token with the dynamic-fee
flag and the ratchet's own immutable tick spacing and hook (LPFeeRatchet.sol:98-106), and poke
derives FDV solely from that pool's TWAP. Nothing stops a third party from creating an unhooked
pool for the same token once it is transferable; only the hooked key is gated, by
AntiSnipeHook._beforeInitialize.
Impact
The committed tier can persistently disagree with the token's real fully diluted valuation. If price
discovery migrates to another venue while the hooked pool stays thin or stale, the ratchet never
advances and the creator retains a higher tier than warranted; alternatively the ratchet is pushed
by cheap activity on the now-isolated pool, which is the same manipulation surface as issue 3
made easier by low liquidity. No principal loss; only the fee split is affected.
Likelihood
Medium for successful tokens, where venue fragmentation is the norm. Low for long-tail launches
whose only market is the hooked pool.
Recommendation
Document that the tier keys to the hooked pool only. If cross-venue FDV matters, blend in an
external oracle or a liquidity-weighted median across known pools.
CrackerSwap Team’s Comment
The tier intentionally keys to the pool this protocol opened, not to the token's global market.
Blending venues would require either a price feed working on four chains before a single launch
can be repriced, with a stale feed then sitting between creators and their fees, or a hardcoded
guess at which pools count. This is the same trade-off FDV_TIERS already makes by pinning USD
thresholds to native wei. The behaviour is documented in ARCHITECTURE.md

9. The closing buyer funds the entire graduation
settlement, uncompensated and without opt-out
Acknowledged
Path
contracts/BondingCurve.sol
Function Name
_buy(), settleGraduation(), graduate(), enterRecovery()
Any buy that pushes realQuote to or above graduationTarget attempts settleGraduation()
atomically inside the same transaction (BondingCurve.sol:311-331). The settlement frame covers
the splitter fee deposit, the token burn, the token transfer, then migration into pool initialisation, a
full-range mint through Permit2, and the NFT handoff with locker validation. It measures 650,781
gas against the 800,000 MIN_SETTLE_GAS floor (:324).
The closer is paid nothing for this. Graduation continuity opens the V4 pool at exactly the price the
closer just paid, so closing carries no arbitrage, and the anti-snipe hook's opening fee taxes any
same-window exit, making close-and-dump unprofitable during the decay window. Meanwhile a buy
just below the target always succeeds, while a crossing buy additionally reverts in full if the caller
leaves less than MIN_SETTLE_GAS at close time. The marginal buyer therefore strictly prefers
staying below the target.
Impact
Graduation depends on altruistic or strategic actors: the creator, the team, or a holder waiting out
the decay window. A curve can idle at more than 99% of target with no forced path across. No
funds are at risk, since sells remain open in TRADING, and once any buy does close the curve
graduate() is permissionless. On the verified chains the subsidy is cents; on an expensive-gas
chain the same structure would make stalls economically rational rather than merely marginal.
Likelihood
Medium that stalls occur transiently; low impact when they do, and self-correcting, since any
holder may close at any time.
Recommendation
Retain the revert (InsufficientGasForSettlement) and preserve atomic graduation. Do not
implement the succeed-and-defer approach.

10. Launch tokens transferred into the curve during
RECOVERY sells are permanently locked
Resolved
Path
contracts/BondingCurve.sol
Function Name
enterRecovery(), sell()
enterRecovery() burns the curve's entire held reserve once, at the moment RECOVERY opens
(BondingCurve.sol:400-401). Every subsequent RECOVERY sell() pulls the seller's tokens into the
curve while paying out the pro-rata claim from tracked state (:365). The incoming tokens are never
burned, re-sold, or otherwise exitable, and accrete in the curve forever.
Impact
Tokens sold back during wind-down are locked rather than burned, so total supply after a recovery
wind-down overstates circulating and burned expectations. Accounting drift only; no value is
extractable. We traced the RECOVERY path specifically for an extraction route and found none:
the pro-rata claim preserves the reserve-to-outstanding ratio, with floor rounding moving it upward
and so favouring later sellers by dust; the guard bounding a sell by the outstanding total limits
redemption to exactly the outstanding supply; and the curve has no path that returns
accumulated tokens.
Likelihood
Certain on any curve that enters RECOVERY and processes sells; impact is accounting-only.
Recommendation
Burn the incoming tokens in the RECOVERY branch of sell(), immediately after the transfer in,
keeping post-mortem supply consistent.

File(s): /vanaPoolStaking/VanaPoolStakingImplementation.sol
Description: Stakers serve a bonding period, during which an early exit returns only the principal and forfeits the accrued rewards. Once
that period has elapsed the position is matured and its rewards are withdrawable. The redelegate(...) function from the VanaPoolStaking
contract lets a staker move a position between entities, and its documentation states that the full share value, principal plus accrued
rewards, travels with the staker and that there is no forfeiture.
When a staker adds to an already matured position through the stake(...) function, the contract first records the matured gain into
vestedRewards and resets the cost basis to the current value, so that the gain can no longer be lost before it re-bonds the position.
1

2
if (stakerEntity.shares > 0) {
3
uint256 oldValue = (stakerEntity.shares * shareToVana) / 1e18;

6

2

3
to.vestedRewards += movedVested;

to.shares += sharesIssued;

previously safe rewards back at risk. If they exit before the newly imposed bond elapses, the unstaking logic takes the bonding branch,
returns only the cost basis, and routes the difference back into the entity’s locked pool for other stakers and the entity owner’s commission.
Recommendation(s): Consider mirroring the logic that the staking path already performs, so that a matured destination position has
its unrealised gain converted into cost basis before any new bonding deadline is applied to it. Consider also reviewing whether the
documented promise that no forfeiture occurs during redelegation holds for every combination of source and destination maturity.

Pushed — c583cc7. Here’s the auditor summary:
[Medium] Redelegating into a matured position makes earned rewards forfeitable — Fixed (commit c583cc7)

existingValue;

and protects A’s matured gain.

matured. This means that if a matured position is redelegated, the rewards become subject to the bounding period again. Consider using
a similar approach to the one used for realizing the rewards for the to’s position.

Issue L-2: WHYPE PM executor is granted the system-
wide HANDLER_ROLE where no existing role is cor-
rectly scoped [RESOLVED]
Source:
https://github.com/sherlock-audit2/2026-08-delpho-update-aug-27th-2026/issues/70
Summary
To let the new WHYPE-market executor pay yield into the shared DelphoRewardDistribut
or, the migration grants it HANDLER_ROLE on the stable ConfigProvider. That is the
broadest hot role in the system: 28 onlyHandler entry points across every stable and
deprecated executor, plus swapAndDistribute. It needs authority over exactly one
function, notifyRewardAmount.
The obvious narrower substitute is also wrong. EXECUTOR_ROLE satisfies DelphoPSM.onlyExe
cutor, which would let a WHYPE-market executor pull USDC from the PSM and break the
rollout's stated market isolation.
Vulnerability Detail
DelphoRewardDistributor resolves roles against its own provider, which after migration is
the stable one, so a WHYPE-market executor needs a stable-provider role to pay in. The
gate accepts either role:
require(config.isHandler(msg.sender)||config.isExecutor(msg.sender) ,
DRD_UNAUTHORIZED());
,→
DelphoConfigProviderMigration.run() and its Safe-calldata twin _buildTxList() satisfy
it with the broader one:
IRoleAdmin(NEW_USDC_CONFIG_PROVIDER).grantRole(stableConfig.HANDLER_ROLE(),
NEW_WHYPE_PM_EXECUTOR);
,→
The intent is narrow: the assertion in _postMigrationChecks() is labelled ”WHYPE PM
reward role missing”. But every executor's onlyHandler modifier resolves isHandler
through the stable provider, so the grant confers authority over 28 functions including cl
awBack, transferFundsToVault, executeCoreAction and the swap extension.
Substituting EXECUTOR_ROLE trades one over-grant for a worse one. DelphoPSM.onlyExecut

original_text:
Cyfrin: Verified.
7.1.4
Sanctioned addresses can be registered as investor or special wallets in breach of OFAC FAQ42
Description: A wallet address enters the protocol through one of two independent registries, and neither consults
the global denylist at any point. A globally denylisted address can therefore be registered as an investor wallet or
assigned a special wallet type after it has been designated.
Investor wallets are held by RegistryService. All three entry points are onlyExchangeOrAbove, except Wal-
letRegistrar::registerWallet which is onlyOwnerOrIssuerOrAbove:
1. RegistryService::addWallet - binds one address to an existing investor, and is the single internal choke
point every investor wallet passes through
2. RegistryService::updateInvestor - iterates its _wallets argument and calls addWallet for each address
not already registered
3. WalletRegistrar::registerWallet - delegates directly to updateInvestor
Special wallets are held by WalletManager. All five entry points are onlyIssuerOrAbove and all funnel into the
internal WalletManager::setSpecialWallet:
4. WalletManager::addIssuerWallet - assigns type ISSUER
5. WalletManager::addIssuerWallets - bulk form, capped at 30 addresses
6. WalletManager::addPlatformWallet - assigns type PLATFORM
7. WalletManager::addPlatformWallets - bulk form, capped at 30 addresses
8. WalletManager::addExchangeWallet - assigns type EXCHANGE, and additionally requires the supplied owner
to hold the exchange role
Both choke points already perform registration-time validation, so the pattern of rejecting an ineligible address at
the point of registration is established. RegistryService::addWallet rejects an address that already carries a
special wallet type and rejects one holding a non-zero balance. WalletManager::setSpecialWallet rejects an
address that already belongs to an investor and rejects a direct type change. The global denylist is simply absent
from both sets of checks.
The global denylist is intended to be a protocol-wide ban expressing sanctions designations.
OFAC FAQ 42
addresses this situation directly and treats onboarding, rather than transacting, as the prohibited act:
What do I do if a person tries to open an account and the individual or entity's name is on OFAC's SDN
List (or is otherwise a blocked person)? Do I open the account and then block the funds?
A U.S. financial institution, its foreign branches, and - in some cases - its wholly-owned or -controlled
foreign subsidiaries, cannot open an account for a person named on OFAC's List of Specially Desig-
nated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN List) or a person who is otherwise blocked (e.g., a blocked
government or an entity that is subject to the 50 Percent Rule). This is a prohibited service.
OFAC FAQ 560 confirms the obligation is identical on-chain:
Are my OFAC compliance obligations the same, regardless of whether a transaction is denominated in
digital currency or traditional fiat currency?
9

Yes, the obligations are the same.
OFAC FAQ 1021 extends it explicitly to wallet-level service providers:
U.S. persons, including virtual currency exchanges, virtual wallet hosts, and other service providers
... are generally prohibited from engaging in or facilitating prohibited transactions, including virtual
currency transactions in which blocked persons have an interest.
Registering a wallet address is the on-chain analogue of opening an account: it is the step that binds an address
to an identity or a role inside the platform and makes it eligible to hold and move a token. The point of FAQ 42
is that the prohibition attaches at that moment, not only when value later moves. A control that screens transfers
but not registration therefore permits the one step FAQ 42 names as prohibited in its own right, and today the only
signal that anything is wrong appears later, when a transfer or issuance involving that wallet is rejected.
Recommended Mitigation: Before registering any new address in the protocol, consult the global deny list and
revert if that address is sanctioned.

whose addWallet is a pure no-op. Since ComplianceServicePermissionless never consults investor-registry
data for authorization in the first place (only the denylist/blacklist checks gate transfers), the fix as suggested would
be dead code on the one compliance path where it could matter.
On special wallets (WalletManager::setSpecialWallet, issuer/platform/exchange) assigning any of these roles
is already gated by onlyIssuerOrAbove a privileged, internal action taken by the issuer/platform operator, not a
customer-facing self-service flow like investor onboarding. Platform/issuer/exchange wallets are Securitize/issuer-
controlled operational infrastructure, not third-party accounts, so the entity granting the role already knows who it's
assigning it to.

File(s): src/Router.sol
Description: A swap carries two output limits. The outputQuote value is the amount the backend quoted, and the outputMin value is the
absolute minimum amount the user must be credited. Two separate features then reduce the amount the executor delivered before that
minimum is checked. When passPositiveSlippageToUser is false, anything above outputQuote is retained by the protocol and the user
is credited exactly outputQuote. When partnerFeeOnOutput is true, the partner fee is denominated in the output token and deducted from
what the user is credited.
The validation accepts any outputMin up to and including outputQuote:
1

2

The execution path then caps the amount, deducts the fee from the capped value, and only afterwards compares against the minimum:

2
if (!params.passPositiveSlippageToUser && amountOut > params.outputQuote) {
3
positiveSlippage = amountOut - params.outputQuote;
4
// @audit The surplus is retained here, so the fee below is charged on
5
// `outputQuote` rather than on the amount the executor delivered.
6
amountOut = params.outputQuote;
7
}
8
9
uint256 outputPartnerFee;
10
if (params.partnerFeeOnOutput && params.partnerFeeBps > 0) {
11
outputPartnerFee = (amountOut * params.partnerFeeBps) / 10_000;
12
// @audit-issue The fee is subtracted from the capped amount.
13
amountOut -= outputPartnerFee;
14
_transferOut(params.outputToken, params.partnerRecipient, outputPartnerFee);
15
}

// @audit-issue The minimum is checked last, against the twice-reduced amount.
18
if (amountOut < params.outputMin) {
19
revert SlippageExceeded(params.outputToken, amountOut, params.outputMin);
20
}

partner fee. Validation, however, allows outputMin all the way up to outputQuote. Every outputMin above the reduced amount therefore
reverts no matter how well the trade executed.
This affects any swap configured with partnerFeeOnOutput set to true, a non-zero partnerFeeBps, and passPositiveSlippageToUser set
to false. With an outputQuote of 1000e18 and a partnerFeeBps of 200, the most the user can be credited is 980e18, so every outputMin
above 980e18 is unreachable. A one percent tolerance places outputMin at 990e18, already inside that range, so the swap cannot succeed.

user pays gas for a transaction that could not have succeeded.

alternatively tightening the validator so that it rejects an outputMin that the configured partnerFeeBps makes unreachable. Whichever
approach is taken should be mirrored in _settleOutputs(...).

Description 
In the validium deposit flow, the replayMessage function re-enqueues the original 
ciphertext at a new queue index, while l2geth selects the encryption key from that new 
index. If the key rotates between a failed deposit and its replay, the decryption attempt 
returns the ErrDecryptionFailed error. l2geth then includes the encrypted call 
unchanged, causing the L2 gateway call to revert before minting and leaving the deposited

Description
The protocol requires its five vault roles (admin, upgrader, operator, certifier, custodian) to be five
different addresses. This is enforced when a vault is created, and creation is rejected if any two match.
One of the shipped migration scripts, which describes itself in its own comments as a live production
migration, hardcodes all five roles to the same address. The vault it tries to create is therefore always
rejected and the script always fails. It has never worked and never will.
Its sibling script does the same thing on purpose and says so plainly in its header, "retained for
controlled failure testing". This one carries no such warning.
Its success checks are also incomplete. It confirms the new vault's pointers, dependencies and roles,
but never checks whether the old vault still holds gold, tokens or pending requests. So if the role
problem were fixed, the script would report success while creating exactly the trapped vault described
in Finding 2.
Impact
Wasted operational effort and a misleading file in the repository. An operator preparing a migration
follows a documented procedure that cannot work, and only finds out when it fails.
Correction to the original report. It claimed the script pauses the live vault before failing, leaving
production frozen with no replacement. That was tested against a real node and does not happen. The
pause step runs during a local dry run, but the tool only sends transactions after the whole script
completes successfully. Since it always fails, nothing is sent and the live system is untouched. This
holds with standard settings and with simulation disabled, and the project's own build commands do not
change it.
So the impact is a broken tool, not a production outage. Severity is Low, not High.
Likelihood
It fails 100% of the time, but the consequence is only wasted time. The dangerous part, the missing
drained vault checks, never runs because the script dies before reaching it.
Recommendation
Read the five role addresses from configuration instead of hardcoding them, and check they are all
different before doing anything else:

bug_title: 3. Re-approving a delayed withdrawal gives the custodian one hour instead of seven days
original_text:
Medium Severity Issues
Medium Severity Issues
3. Re-approving a delayed withdrawal gives the custodian
one hour instead of seven days
Acknowledged
Path
src/VaultManager.sol
Description
When an operator approves a gold withdrawal, a seven day clock starts. If the custodian has not shipped
within that window, the customer may cancel and take their tokens back.
Operators can also revoke an approval, which is the documented way to handle a shipping delay and re-
assign later. Revoking resets the status and clears several fields, but it does not reset the clock. When
the request is approved again, the original seven day deadline is still running.
So an operator can re-approve on day 6 and what looks like a fresh seven day window is actually one
hour. The custodian sees a new approval and has no reason to suspect otherwise.
There is a second problem in the same place, not in the original report. If the request is left revoked past
the seven day mark it can never be approved again, because the system rejects it as expired. An
operator using the documented delay procedure can permanently destroy a customer's ability to
receive their gold. Only cancel or reject remain.
Impact
The customer ends up with both the gold and the money. Once the stale deadline passes they cancel
and get a 100% refund, while the bar has already shipped. The books then count that bar as backing
again, so the shortfall is invisible and the health check reports full solvency.
This is the same end state as Finding 1, reached through a different door.
The second problem is a service failure rather than a loss: a withdrawal becomes permanently
unfulfillable and must be torn down and restarted.
Likelihood
Medium. It needs an operator to use revoke and re-approve late in the window, which is exactly what
that flow exists for, since delayed international bullion shipments are the reason it is there.
The customer plans nothing. They cancel when the system allows it, which looks completely legitimate
from their side. The custodian gets caught out and has no on chain signal that the window is closing.
The docs acknowledge that cancel and complete can race after the deadline. What they do not
acknowledge, and what makes this a finding, is that revoke and re-approve silently compresses the
window without telling anyone.

Description
The RemoteHopV201Tempo.sendOFT function copies the caller-supplied final recipient into
HopMessage and pulls principal without validating that recipient:
HopMessage memory hopMessage = HopMessage({
srcEid: $.localEid,
dstEid: _dstEid,
dstGas: _dstGas,
sender: bytes32(uint256(uint160(msg.sender))),
recipient: _recipient,
data: _data
});
_amountLD = removeDust(_oft, _amountLD);
if (_amountLD > 0) ITIP20(IOFT(_oft).token()).transferFrom(msg.sender,
address(this), _amountLD);
No hop or wrapper entry point rejects bytes32(0) or a nonzero value whose low 160 bits decode
to address(0). The outcome depends on the route:
• A same-chain local send reaches _sendLocal and reverts atomically.
• An empty-data remote route eventually uses the final recipient as an outer OFT
SendParam.to, exposing the transport-layer failure described separately.
• A data-bearing route addresses the OFT message to a valid hop and keeps the final
recipient inside HopMessage. Destination credit succeeds, but later lzCompose retries all
revert when _sendLocal decodes the nested recipient to zero.
An outer OFT recipient check cannot detect the composed case because the OFT sees only the
valid hop address.

Impact
The initiating caller can commit its principal to an unusable remote intent. On a composed route,
principal remains credited to the destination hop while the immutable nested recipient causes
every compose retry to fail; recovery or compensation then requires administrator action.
The caller chooses the recipient and funds the transfer. No path was found to alter another user's
recipient or debit a passive holder.
Recommendations
Validate the final recipient consistently in hop and wrapper quote/send paths, before any token
pull or fee collection. Reject bytes32(0) universally, and reject low-160-bit-zero values when the
final destination is EVM.
